title: Green's Shim Sham Shimmy and Dancer's Night at Connie's Inn
summary: Green dances his version of the Shim Sham Shimmy and explains choreographer Teddy Blackman, Connie Immerman's Dancer's Night and the prizes given out.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well, did you have a particular way of doing it yourself?
Oh, yeah, I had a particular way, yes.
That's a natural introduction to your doing it for us.
Well, I'll let you see it.
So, this is Chuck Green's version of the Shim Sham Shimmy.
That was very nice. (Recording interruption) Tell me a little bit about the Shim Sham Shimmy and how that reflected the personality of tap dancing.

Well, it reflected the personality of tap dancing because the chorus girls finally took an encore. Mr. Teddy Blackman -- he was the choreographer at that time at the Lafayette Theater, and sometimes he would go around into Connie's Carny's Inn and assist Mr. Clarence Robinson Robertson, which was another famous choreographer. He did shows for the Carny's Inn and the Cotton Club also -- mostly in the night clubs like Small's Paradise and sometime he did a lot of work for Ziegfield -- Florenz Ziegfield's choreography. And the Shim-Sham Shimmy -- Connie Mr. Carny Immerman who owned the Carny's Inn -- was named after him -- he got this idea of having a dancer's night and because the Shim Sham-Shimmy became famous, everybody wanted to learn it and mostly the people -- the public. They liked to dance and they liked the steps. It was like an education dance. It was a tap dance, you see, and he got this idea of having a

dancer's night. Like when a celebrity -- a lot of celebrities used to come into Connie's Inn -- and they came to Harlem a lot at that time into these night clubs, and you may see anyone there, you see. You may see Dick Powell, the great singer, (Laughter) and some great band leader or somebody known dancers or whoever, you know. It was the master of ceremonies who made the show more entertaining, you see, because the dancer's night occurred after the first part of the show, like during the intermission, see. And that's when they would have dancer's night. And they used to give away like cakes, a bouquet of flowers, cartons of cigarettes, some kind of cases of -- of course, prohibition was in, you see -- some what they call happy juice, see. And that way it was always an entertainment to see someone trying to do the Shim Sham Shimmy -- a different way than it originally was, which was an education dance. But if someone had only observed it and never tried or attempted to demonstrate the Shim-Sham Shimmy, that's where you would bet the happiness of seeing them doing their education dance, you see. (Recording interruption) Yeah, that was on account of the popularity of the dance, and this night became popular also by being named Dancer's Night. So, that's why when the dancers would meet in the street they would say, "Shim Sham," because they were making fun of each other, like, "Are you going to go down to Connie's Connie's Carny's Inn tonight?" See, Connie's Inn was an interracial night club up there in Harlem, same as Small's Paradise and so

on, Uptown House, Rockham Palace, Elk's Rendezvous, Savoy Ballroom, you know. This dance became popular and most dancers would always try to do -- this is the version of someone else doing -- a version of the Shim-Sham Shimmy during Dancer's Night. It was always trying to give tap dancing a new degree, that's actually what they were trying to do, see. Like a wing tap dancer would probably do the Shim-Sham Shimmy their version in wings, see. Over-the-top tap dancer would do Shim-Sham Shimmy in their version of wings over-the-top, you see.
We'll have you demonstrate an over-the-top and through the trenches a little bit later on.
Because those are definitely very important steps.
